text:
Burnout recovery is often measured in years, not weeks. That changes what "ready to go back" means.

In Practice, issue 12, is now live.

In Practice is our one-page research update for GPs and anyone working in primary care. This issue looks at why burnout recovery is often measured in years, not weeks.

What the issue covers:
1. Long-term follow-up of people treated for clinical burnout: most improved, but few felt fully recovered years later.
2. What research in healthy workers shows about holidays: the lift fades after the return to work.
3. Why "better" is not the same as "recovered", and what to listen for at review.
4. Three questions for the consult, and when to consider a referral.

The patient handout, Burnout recovery, explains why rest alone may not be enough and offers small, practical steps. Both are free to download from our referrers page: https://equalpsychology.com.au/referrers#in-practice

Key sources:
World Health Organization. (2019). Burn-out an "occupational phenomenon": International Classification of Diseases. https://www.who.int/news-room/detail/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases
Glise, K., Wiegner, L., & Jonsdottir, I. H. (2020). Long-term follow-up of residual symptoms in patients treated for stress-related exhaustion. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-020-0395-8
Eskilsson, T., Olsson, D., Ekbäck, A.-M., & Slunga Järvholm, L. (2024). Symptoms, work situation and work functioning 10 years after rehabilitation of stress-induced exhaustion disorder. BMC Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-024-05975-x
